title: Zero-Touch CI/CD Pipeline to EKS
tagline: Push to main, watch it land in production.
description: A fully automated pipeline that takes a commit from GitHub through build, security scan, and deploy into an Amazon EKS cluster — no manual kubectl apply, ever.

details.overview: This project automates the full lifecycle of a containerized application: every push triggers a build, a static code scan, an image vulnerability scan, and a rolling deploy to a Kubernetes cluster on AWS, provisioned entirely with Terraform.
details.architecture: GitHub Actions runs on push → builds a Docker image → SonarQube scans code quality → Trivy scans the image for CVEs → image is pushed to ECR → a Helm chart is applied to an EKS cluster provisioned by Terraform → rollout status is verified before the job is marked green.
features: One command Terraform provisioning for the entire EKS cluster and VPC
Automated image vulnerability scanning that fails the build on critical CVEs
Blue/green style rolling deployments with automatic rollback on failed health checks
Slack notification on deploy success or failure
folderStructure: infra/ – Terraform modules for VPC, EKS, IAM
helm/ – Helm chart for the application
lessonsLearned: IAM least-privilege for CI service accounts is worth the extra setup time
Rollout health checks matter more than the deploy step itself
challenges: Getting Terraform state locking right across multiple environments
Tuning readiness probes so rollbacks triggered fast enough to matter
futureImprovements: Swap manual Helm apply for ArgoCD-driven GitOps
Add canary deployments with automated traffic shifting

title: Kubernetes Observability Stack
tagline: If it's running in the cluster, I can see it.
description: A self-hosted monitoring stack for Kubernetes bringing metrics, dashboards, and alerting together for every workload in the cluster.

details.overview: A learning-focused project to stand up a production-shaped observability stack: Prometheus scraping cluster and application metrics, Grafana dashboards for visualization, and alerting rules for the failure modes that actually matter.
details.architecture: Prometheus Operator deployed via Helm scrapes node-exporter and kube-state-metrics, plus custom application metrics exposed on /metrics. Grafana reads from Prometheus as a data source and renders pre-built dashboards. Alertmanager routes critical alerts to Slack.
features: Pre-built Grafana dashboards for node, pod, and application-level metrics
Custom alerting rules for pod crash loops and memory pressure
Helm values file to toggle which exporters get deployed
lessonsLearned: Cardinality matters — over-labeling metrics quietly kills Prometheus performance
A good dashboard answers a question, it doesn't just display numbers
challenges: Right-sizing Prometheus storage retention on a small home lab cluster
Writing alert rules with just enough sensitivity to not create alert fatigue
futureImprovements: Add Loki for log aggregation alongside metrics
Wire alerts into an on-call rotation tool

title: GitOps Delivery with ArgoCD
tagline: Git is the single source of truth. ArgoCD makes sure the cluster agrees.
description: A GitOps workflow where every cluster change starts as a pull request, and ArgoCD continuously reconciles the live cluster state to match Git.

details.overview: A small but complete GitOps setup: application manifests live in a Git repo, ArgoCD watches that repo, and any drift between the repo and the live cluster gets automatically corrected.
details.architecture: ArgoCD Application resources point at a Git repo containing Helm charts. On every merge to main, ArgoCD detects the diff and syncs the cluster. Manual `kubectl edit` on any resource gets reverted automatically on the next reconciliation loop.
features: Self-healing deployments — manual cluster edits get reverted to match Git
App-of-apps pattern to manage multiple services from one root application
Sync waves to control deployment order across dependent services
folderStructure: environments/ – dev and staging value overrides
lessonsLearned: GitOps changes how you think about incidents — you fix the repo, not the cluster
Sync waves are essential once services have real dependencies between them
challenges: Understanding ArgoCD's reconciliation loop timing during first setup
Structuring the repo so dev and staging don't fight over the same values
futureImprovements: Add ArgoCD Notifications for Slack sync status
Introduce progressive delivery with Argo Rollouts

title: Dockerized MERN Stack Deployment
tagline: One docker-compose up, four services, zero setup docs needed.
description: A full MERN application containerized with Docker Compose, reverse-proxied through NGINX, ready to run identically on a laptop or a server.

details.overview: A MERN stack application (MongoDB, Express, React, Node) fully containerized so that the exact same environment runs in development and production, with NGINX handling reverse proxy and static asset serving.
details.architecture: docker-compose orchestrates four services: a MongoDB container with a named volume for persistence, a Node/Express API container, a React frontend built into static assets, and an NGINX container reverse-proxying API calls and serving the frontend.
features: Single command startup for the entire stack
Named volumes so database data survives container restarts
NGINX reverse proxy routing /api to the backend and everything else to the frontend build
Environment-based configuration via .env files, never hardcoded
lessonsLearned: Multi-stage Docker builds cut the final image size dramatically
Named volumes vs bind mounts matters a lot for database durability
challenges: Getting NGINX to correctly proxy WebSocket connections for hot reload in dev
Keeping build times reasonable with proper Docker layer caching
futureImprovements: Add a docker-compose.prod.yml with resource limits
Move to a Kubernetes deployment for the same stack

title: Reusable Terraform AWS VPC Module
tagline: Infrastructure you can read like documentation.
description: A parameterized Terraform module that stands up a production-shaped VPC — public/private subnets, NAT, route tables, and security groups — in one apply.

details.overview: A reusable, parameterized Terraform module for standing up a secure AWS VPC: public and private subnets across multiple availability zones, a NAT gateway for outbound-only traffic, and security groups scoped to least privilege.
details.architecture: Root module composes smaller modules for subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and security groups. Variables control the number of AZs, CIDR ranges, and whether a NAT gateway is single or one-per-AZ.
features: Multi-AZ public and private subnet layout out of the box
Configurable single NAT gateway or one-per-AZ for high availability
Sensible default security groups with clearly documented overrides
folderStructure: examples/basic/ – a working example root module
lessonsLearned: Good module variables read like a checklist for what actually varies between environments
One-NAT-per-AZ is a cost decision as much as a reliability one
challenges: Designing variable defaults that are safe without being opinionated to the point of being unusable
Writing documentation clear enough that future-me doesn't need to re-read the source
futureImprovements: Publish the module to the Terraform Registry
Add automated `terraform plan` checks in CI on every PR

title: Jenkins Multibranch Pipeline with Quality Gates
tagline: Every branch gets the same bar to clear.
description: A Jenkins multibranch pipeline enforcing code quality and dependency security checks before any branch can be merged.

details.overview: A Jenkins multibranch pipeline that builds every branch with Maven, runs a SonarQube quality gate, checks dependencies with OWASP Dependency Check, and publishes passing artifacts to Nexus.
details.architecture: Jenkinsfile defines stages for build, unit tests, SonarQube analysis, dependency check, and artifact publish. The pipeline fails fast on any quality gate breach, before an artifact ever reaches Nexus.
features: Automatic pipeline creation for every new branch via multibranch scan
Hard quality gate — a failing SonarQube scan blocks the merge
Dependency vulnerability report attached to every build
lessonsLearned: Quality gates only work if they're enforced in the pipeline, not just displayed on a dashboard
Caching the local Maven repo between builds saves real pipeline time
challenges: Tuning SonarQube's quality gate thresholds so they catch real issues without blocking every branch
Getting Jenkins credentials scoped correctly per-branch for the Nexus publish step
futureImprovements: Migrate the pipeline definition to run in a containerized Jenkins agent
Add Trivy image scanning once the app is containerized
